mcqs.question: Two candidates both submit take-homes that pass every automated grading check. Why might they still receive very different scores?
options: The evaluator scores based on judgment visible in the code and README, not just whether checks pass
Automated checks are only a formality and are never actually reviewed
One candidate's solution must contain a hidden bug the checks failed to catch
Scores are randomized to account for grader fatigue across submissions
mcqs.explanation: A take-home strips out the live observation an interviewer would normally get, so the artifact itself has to carry that signal — prioritization, what was cut, test coverage of risky paths. Passing checks is necessary but not sufficient; there's no reason to assume a hidden bug or random scoring.

mcqs.question: A take-home prompt mentions offhand that "this service will eventually run in production" but never lists logging or error handling as requirements. What should you take from that?
options: Ignore it since it isn't in the explicit requirements list
Treat it as an implicit signal and add reasonable logging and error handling without being asked
Email the company asking them to add it to the explicit requirements
Assume it's boilerplate language with no bearing on grading
mcqs.explanation: Implicit signals are often more informative than the explicit checklist — a phrase like that is testing whether you add production concerns unprompted. Ignoring it or dismissing it as boilerplate misses exactly the judgment being evaluated.

mcqs.question: Why set a time budget for planning before writing any code, even though it feels like it steals time from building?
options: It's mainly a formality reviewers expect to see mentioned in the README
Planning time doesn't count against the suggested duration
Skipping it risks building the wrong thing well, which costs far more time than planning would have
It's only useful for open-ended prompts, not time-boxed ones
mcqs.explanation: A short planning phase is what catches a misread requirement before it costs an hour of wasted code. It counts fully against your budget and matters for both time-boxed and open-ended prompts, not just one type.

mcqs.question: You realize the take-home would benefit from rate limiting but don't have time to build it. What's the strongest move?
options: Silently skip it and hope the evaluator doesn't notice the gap
Explicitly note in the README what you'd add and why, without building it
Add a stub function that does nothing but is named rateLimiter
Spend the remaining time budget building a minimal version instead of testing what you have
mcqs.explanation: Naming the gap and reasoning about the fix shows judgment even without the code existing. A silent skip risks reading as not noticing; an empty stub is misleading; and spending remaining budget on a new feature over testing existing code is a scope-management mistake.

mcqs.question: A prompt suggests 4 hours but a candidate spends 3 days adding a plugin architecture and 100% test coverage. How does this typically read to evaluators?
options: As strong diligence and above-and-beyond effort
As neutral, since more code is never a negative
As proof the candidate needs less onboarding time
As poor judgment about scope and time, the opposite of the signal intended
mcqs.explanation: Effort mismatched to the problem's actual scope is exactly the failure mode this pitfall names — it signals the candidate might gold-plate real tickets too, not that they're diligent. More code and time spent are not neutral; they're a negative signal when they exceed the stated scope.
